problemText: What does the word elevation mean in geography? Choose the best definition.
choices: How high a point of land sits above sea level
How much the height of the land changes across an area
How steep the hills are near a town
How far a place is from the nearest ocean
hints: Think about the word 'level' — elevation is measured up from a standard starting point.
Sea level is the shared reference line used for all elevations on Earth.

problemText: A place is described as sitting 150 meters above sea level, with the ground staying nearly the same height for miles around it. What is the elevation and relief of this place?
choices: High elevation and high relief
Low elevation and low relief
Low elevation and high relief
High elevation and low relief
hints: 150 meters is a small distance above sea level compared to mountains — is that high or low?
If the ground stays nearly the same height for miles around, is that much change or little change?

problemText: Two places both sit about 2,000 meters above sea level. Place A has ground that stays almost level for a long stretch. Place B has ground that rises and falls sharply within a short distance. Which statement is true?
choices: Both places have the same elevation and the same relief
The places have different elevations but the same relief
Both places have the same elevation but different relief
The places have different elevations and different relief
hints: If both places sit at about 2,000 meters above sea level, what does that tell you about their elevations?
The descriptions of the ground around each place are different — so check relief by itself, separate from elevation.

problemText: A student says: 'Highcliff sits 3,000 meters above sea level, so it must have high relief with steep cliffs and sharp drops all around it.' Highcliff is actually described this way: it sits 3,000 meters above sea level, but the ground around it stays nearly flat and level for a long stretch in every direction. What is wrong with the student's reasoning, and what is the correct description of Highcliff?
choices: The student mixed up the definitions of elevation and relief. Highcliff has low elevation and low relief.
The student wrongly assumed that high elevation means high relief. Highcliff has low elevation and high relief.
The student was correct that high elevation always means high relief. Highcliff must have high relief.
The student wrongly assumed that high elevation means high relief. Highcliff has high elevation and low relief.
hints: Look at what the student did — they looked at the elevation (3,000 meters) and then guessed about the relief without reading what the ground is actually like.
The description says the ground stays nearly flat and level — what does that tell you about relief, no matter how high the place sits?

problemText: Deepvalley sits about 80 meters above sea level. The ground right around Deepvalley rises steeply on all sides, with deep dips and sharp climbs. Plainridge sits about 1,800 meters above sea level. The ground around Plainridge changes very little, staying nearly the same height for miles. Which place has the higher elevation, and which place has the higher relief?
choices: Plainridge has higher elevation; Deepvalley has higher relief
Deepvalley has higher elevation and higher relief
Deepvalley has higher elevation; Plainridge has higher relief
Plainridge has higher elevation and higher relief
hints: Answer the elevation question first by comparing the heights above sea level: 80 meters versus 1,800 meters.
Answer the relief question second by checking each description separately: one place has sharp changes, the other has little change.

problemText: Three places are described below. Use the elevation and relief of each to sort them correctly. Mesa View sits 2,200 meters above sea level with ground that stays nearly level. Craggy Peak sits 2,100 meters above sea level with ground that rises and falls sharply nearby. Flatshore sits 5 meters above sea level with ground that stays nearly level. Which statement correctly places all three places by their elevation, and separately by their relief?
choices: By elevation from highest to lowest: Craggy Peak, Mesa View, Flatshore. By relief from high to low: Craggy Peak, Flatshore, Mesa View.
By elevation from highest to lowest: Mesa View, Craggy Peak, Flatshore. By relief from high to low: Craggy Peak, Mesa View, Flatshore.
By elevation from highest to lowest: Craggy Peak, Flatshore, Mesa View. By relief from high to low: Mesa View, Craggy Peak, Flatshore.
By elevation from highest to lowest: Flatshore, Craggy Peak, Mesa View. By relief from high to low: Mesa View, Flatshore, Craggy Peak.
hints: Start with elevation alone: line up the three heights above sea level (2,200, 2,100, and 5 meters) from highest to lowest. Then ignore elevation completely and check only the relief descriptions.
Remember that a place can sit higher than another but still have less relief — you must check both facts separately for each place.

problemText: A piece of land is completely surrounded by water on all sides and has no connection to any larger landmass. What is this landform called?
choices: Isthmus
Peninsula
Island
Coast
hints: Think about what happens when you trace the entire edge of this piece of land.
This landform has no way to reach it by land — you must cross water no matter which direction you come from.

problemText: In a made-up region, a narrow strip of land has ocean water along its entire north side and ocean water along its entire south side. At its western end, the strip widens into a larger area of land. At its eastern end, it runs out into open ocean with no additional land beyond it. What is this narrow strip of land?
choices: An isthmus, because water runs along both long sides
A coast, because it touches ocean water on its edges where land meets the sea
An island, because it has water on two sides and is surrounded by ocean on multiple edges
A peninsula, because it is attached to land on one end and surrounded by water on the other end
hints: Check what sits at each end of the narrow strip — does one end lead to more land and the other to water, or do both ends lead to land?
An isthmus must have land at both ends; a peninsula ends in water on all sides but one.

problemText: A mapmaker describes a landform in an invented country called Meridia: water touches its north, south, and east edges completely. On its west edge, it connects without any water break to the rest of Meridia. Which of the following correctly names and explains this landform?
choices: It is a peninsula because three of its sides have water but it is still attached to a larger landmass on one side
It is an island because water surrounds three of its edges, which means it is completely separated from all other land areas
It is an isthmus because it has water on both its long sides and connects two separate landmasses together at their edges
It is a coast because water meets the land at multiple edges and this boundary creates the shoreline along three directions
hints: Count how many sides touch water and how many sides stay connected to land.
A peninsula must be attached to a larger landmass on one side — the side that is not water.

problemText: Two narrow strips of land exist in a region called Vestor. Strip A has water along its north and south sides and connects two larger areas of land — one at its west end and one at its east end. Strip B has water along its north and south sides, connects to a larger area of land at its west end, but at its east end it simply ends in open water. Both strips touch ocean water, but which statement correctly distinguishes between them?
choices: Strip A is a peninsula and Strip B is an isthmus; both are narrow with water on two sides, so the names are interchangeable depending on location
Strip A is an isthmus and Strip B is a peninsula; an isthmus connects two separate areas of land while a peninsula ends in water on all sides but one
Both are isthmuses because both have water running along their long sides and both are narrow strips of land
Strip A is a coast and Strip B is a coast; they are the same landform because both touch ocean water and both have coasts running along their edges
hints: Use the one-question check: does the narrow strip lead to more land at its far end, or does it leave you surrounded by water there?
An isthmus must have larger land areas at both of its ends; a peninsula dead-ends in water everywhere except the one side it is attached by.

problemText: A student claims: 'A coast is a kind of island, because an island has water all around it, and that water edge is the coast.' Identify the error in this student's thinking and explain why it is incorrect, using the definitions of both terms.
choices: The error is correct; a coast is indeed a type of island because both involve water touching the land
The error is not understanding that an island has no connection to other land while a coast is simply the edge where land meets water, not a landform category itself

The error is confusing the definition of coast with the shape of a landform. Coast names the edge itself where land meets an ocean or sea, not a shape. An island is a shape defined by water surrounding it on all sides. Every island has a coast, but a coast is not a type of island — it is a feature that can exist on any landform that touches an ocean or sea
The error is thinking that only islands have coasts; in fact, coasts only form where mainlands meet the ocean and islands cannot have coasts
hints: Think about whether 'coast' and 'island' answer the same question about a piece of land.
Coast answers the question 'Where does land meet ocean?' Island answers the question 'How much water surrounds this land and what is it attached to?'

problemText: In an imaginary archipelago region, there are three landforms: Landform X is a large mainland area. Landform Y is a narrow strip of land with ocean on both its long sides that connects Landform X on the west to an entirely separate mainland called Altara on the east. Landform Z is another narrow strip of land with ocean on both its long sides that connects Landform X on the west, but at its east end it simply terminates in open ocean. A student says all three landforms have coasts, and all three can be named by a single term. Which statement best evaluates this claim?
choices: The student is correct. All three have coasts because all three touch ocean water, and all three are types of land connected to continents
The student is correct about the coasts but confused about structure. All three have coasts and all three should be called isthmuses because they have water on multiple sides
The student is partly wrong. Only Landform X is a mainland with a coast; Landforms Y and Z have no coasts because they are surrounded by water on their sides

The student is partly correct about coasts but wrong about the single term. All three touch ocean, so all have coasts. However, Landform Y is an isthmus, Landform Z is a peninsula, and Landform X is a mainland — three different names because their structure is different
hints: Separate the two parts of the student's claim: first check whether all three have coasts, then check whether they can all be named by one term by examining what is at each end of the narrow strips.
Remember that coast is a different kind of word than island, peninsula, and isthmus — it answers a location question, not a shape question.

problemText: A landform rises steeply above the land around it and comes to a narrow, pointed top. Which landform is this?
choices: A hill
A mountain
A plateau
A plain
hints: Does this landform stand HIGH and come to a point, or does it stay LOW and flat?
Think about whether the top is narrow and steep or rounded and gentle.

problemText: You are told that a stretch of land stands much higher than the country around it, but its surface stays flat across a wide area instead of narrowing to a point. Which landform does this describe? Explain why this cannot be a mountain.
choices: A plain, because plains are flat surfaces that extend across wide areas without rising higher than the surrounding land
A mountain, because anything that stands high must be a mountain
A plateau, because it is high but flat on top, not high and pointed like a mountain
A hill, because it rises above the surrounding land and has a rounded shape rather than steep cliffs
hints: A mountain needs TWO properties: to stand high AND to narrow to a peak. Does this landform have both?
What does a plateau's flat top tell you about why this is not a mountain?

problemText: Two landforms both rise above the land around them. One climbs steeply with slopes that are sharp and rocky, while the other rises more gently with rounded, rolling slopes. The steep one reaches much higher than the gentle one. Which is the hill and which is the mountain?
choices: Both are hills because the gently rolling one is definitely a hill
The gentle, rolling one is the mountain; the steep one is the hill
Both are mountains because they both stand above their surroundings
The steep, high one is the mountain; the gentle, lower one is the hill
hints: Remember that both height and the shape of the slopes matter when sorting mountains from hills.
A mountain is high AND steep; a hill is lower AND has gentler slopes. Which description fits which landform?

problemText: Three regions of invented land are described. Region A is a low, flat stretch that goes on for many miles with almost no change in how high the land is. Region B is low ground that runs like a strip between two high ridges, one ridge on each side. Region C is high land with steep drop-offs around its edges, but its top surface is mostly flat. A student says 'Regions A and B are the same landform because they are both low.' Explain what is wrong with this claim, and name each landform correctly.
choices: The claim is wrong because a valley is defined not just by being low, but by having higher land on both sides, while a plain is just a wide level area; Region A is a plain, Region B is a valley, Region C is a plateau

The claim is wrong because plains are defined by their flat surface and lack of bordering ridges, while valleys require high ground pressed in on both sides; Region A is a valley, Region B is a plain, Region C is a mountain
The claim is wrong because a plain can have ridges embedded in it, while a valley must run between two distinct boundaries; Region A is a plain, Region B is a plateau, Region C is a mountain

The claim is wrong because Region B is squeezed between high land on both sides while Region A spreads across open flat land with no required boundaries; Region A is a plateau, Region B is a valley, Region C is a plain
hints: A valley is not just 'low'—it must be low AND squeezed between higher land. A plain is just a wide flat area with no special requirement about what borders it.
For Region C, check the two sorting questions: Does it stand high? Is its top flat or pointed?

problemText: A student draws a picture of a landform and labels it 'This is a mountain because it is the highest point in the area.' But when you read the description, the landform has a flat, level surface across its top that stretches for miles, with steep cliffs only at the edges. Why is the student's naming wrong, and what is the correct name?
choices: The student is correct; the highest point must always be a mountain by definition
The student checked only height, not the shape of the top; the correct name is a plateau because it is high but flat across its surface, not narrow and peaked like a mountain
The student did not check whether it has ridges; the correct name is a hill because it has a flat top instead of a peak, which means it does not meet the definition of a mountain
The student named it wrong because it has steep edges; the correct name is a valley because valleys also have steep boundaries and are surrounded by high ground on multiple sides
hints: What two questions must you ask about any landform to name it correctly? Did the student ask both?
A mountain is high AND narrows to a point. Does the landform in the picture have both of those properties?

problemText: An invented continent has five regions described only by words, with no pictures or maps. Region 1: 'The land is flat and open, stretching for hundreds of miles with only gentle ups and downs.' Region 2: 'A strip of low ground runs north to south, with a tall rocky ridge on its west side and another tall ridge on its east side.' Region 3: 'The land rises gradually to rounded slopes that reach a height of a few thousand feet, then flattens out.' Region 4: 'Steep rocky walls climb thousands of feet straight up from the base, and at the top sits a narrow peak.' Region 5: 'High, level ground covers a large area, with cliffs dropping away at the edges.' A student must sort these five regions into the five landform types without seeing any pictures. Which region is a hill, and which two regions could never be confused because they have opposite answers to both sorting questions?
choices: Region 3 is the hill; Regions 1 and 2 have opposite answers because 1 is flat and not between higher land while 2 is low and between higher land
Region 2 is the hill; Regions 4 and 5 have opposite answers because 4 is high and pointed while 5 is high and flat
Region 3 is the hill; Regions 4 and 5 have opposite answers because 4 is high and pointed while 5 is high and flat
Region 1 is the hill; Regions 2 and 4 have opposite answers because 2 is a valley and 4 is a mountain
hints: A hill rises above its surroundings but less far and more gently than a mountain does. Which description matches that pattern?
Two regions could never be confused if they give opposite answers to at least one of the two sorting questions. Region 4 is high and pointed. Which other region is high but NOT pointed?

problemText: A body of water has land completely surrounding it on every side, and no part of its edge opens onto an ocean or a sea. Based on the defining property of this water feature, what is it called?
choices: A river
A gulf
A strait
A lake
hints: Think about which water feature is enclosed on all sides with no opening to the ocean.
The defining property here is complete enclosure by land.

problemText: Water moves downhill through a narrow channel cut into the ground, flowing from mountains toward lower elevation. Along the way, it passes through forests and meadows. At the end of its path, it empties into a large ocean. What water feature is this water, and why?
choices: A river, because water that flows downhill through a channel across the land from higher to lower ground defines a river
A strait, because it is a narrow passage connecting two bodies of salt water that allows movement from one ocean region to another
A gulf, because it is enclosed by land on most sides with an opening to a larger body of water and receives freshwater input from streams
A lake, because it is a body of water surrounded by natural landscape features such as forests, meadows, and mountains on its shores
hints: Ask yourself: is the water flowing through a channel from high ground to low ground?
The defining property of a river is its movement, not where it ends up or what surrounds it.

problemText: A stretch of salt water connects to the ocean through one narrower opening. Land curves around three sides of this body of water, and a ship sailing in from the ocean must exit through that same narrow opening it entered. Which water feature fits this description?
choices: A strait
A gulf
A river
A sea
hints: Notice that a ship enters and exits through the same opening—not passing all the way through to a different body of water.
A gulf is a pocket of salt water with land mostly around it and one narrow opening back to the ocean.

problemText: Two invented water features are described below. Water Feature X: salt water with land on both sides, where a ship can enter from one ocean and sail straight through to come out into a different ocean on the opposite side. Water Feature Y: water completely enclosed by land with no opening to any ocean or sea. Explain why Water Feature X is not a gulf and why Water Feature Y is not a gulf.
choices: Water Feature X is not a gulf because it is too narrow, and Water Feature Y is not a gulf because it is freshwater instead of salt water
Water Feature X is a sea because it touches two oceans, and Water Feature Y is a river because water is completely enclosed

Water Feature X is a strait because it connects two different bodies of water end to end, not a pocket entered and exited from the same side; Water Feature Y is a lake because it has no opening to the ocean at all, while a gulf always has exactly one
Water Feature X is a strait because it is salty, and Water Feature Y is a lake because it has no moving current
hints: For X, think about whether a ship enters and exits the same way or passes through to somewhere else entirely.
For Y, ask whether a gulf can be completely closed off from the ocean or whether it must have one opening.

problemText: A student claims that a certain body of salt water must be a sea because it is very large. Another student claims that a different body of salt water must be a gulf because land surrounds most of it. Which student's reasoning is correct according to the definitions taught, and why?
choices: The first student is correct because size is the most important factor in distinguishing a sea from a gulf or other water features
The second student is correct because having land on all sides except one opening is the only reliable way to identify a gulf accurately
Both students are correct because their observations—large size and surrounding land—are the key ways to tell the difference between a sea and a gulf

Neither student is using correct reasoning, because size alone does not define a sea, and surrounding land alone does not define a gulf; the defining properties are how broadly or narrowly the water connects to the ocean
hints: Recall that neither a sea nor a gulf is defined by how large it is.
A sea and a gulf are both distinguished by the width and openness of their connection to the ocean, not just by how much land is around them.

problemText: An explorer describes three water features in a newly mapped region. Feature A is completely surrounded by land with no ocean opening anywhere. Feature B flows continuously downhill through a channel and empties into Feature A. Feature C is salt water bordered by land on one side with a broad, open connection to the larger ocean on the other. Now imagine Feature B were to reverse direction and flow out of Feature A instead of into it. Would Feature A still be the same type of water feature, or would it have to be reclassified? Explain your reasoning using the definition that matters.
choices: Feature A would still be the same type because its defining property—being completely enclosed by land with no ocean opening—would not change, regardless of which direction water flows in or out of it through Feature B
Feature A would become a gulf because water flowing out through Feature B would create a connection to the ocean on one side with land surrounding the other sides
Feature A would become a strait because the bidirectional flow of Feature B would allow water to pass between two separate bodies of water in either direction
Feature A would become a sea because reversing the flow would change the salinity and size of the enclosed water body significantly enough to meet sea classification standards
hints: Think about what the defining property of Feature A's water type actually is—is it the direction of flow, or is it the enclosure itself?
Remember that a river flowing in or out of a lake does not change the lake into a river; the river is a separate channel, and the lake's enclosure is what matters.
